utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Krsnik, for you to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. If I remember correctly, my last question yesterday had to do with the security or intelligence service with the acronym of SIS. And if I'm not mistaken, you said you were familiar with the acronym, with the name.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard that name before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know what the purview of SIS is? I'm sorry. It's SIS in the transcript but I that's not what I said. H-I-S, HIS. The same goes for the first question. Let me repeat: Are you familiar with the purview of the security service?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in any depth at all, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know and did you enter the archives of the said security services during your work, and are you familiar with the service called UNS?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been in the archives, no. And can you repeat the last part?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A service called U-N-S, UNS.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in understanding from your answers that you do not know anything about the subordination, chain, or chain of command of the services mentioned thus far?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in any detail, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us conclude this part of my questioning. With the help of the usher and with some assistance from my friends from the Prosecution, I would like to put in front of you this visual aid based on the document prepared by the Prosecution concerning Hrvatski List newspaper. OTP 4. [In English] You can put on the ELMO also. Mr. Usher. Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, we could show that on Sanction potentially, as an alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I agree. Certainly. Binder 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which one are you referring to, Mr. Krsnik? OTP 4 seems to me to be a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is a statement, and it was marked OTP 4, Exhibit OTP 4. Your Honour, I will have Hrvatski List parallel with the exhibit now called OTP 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, to clarify, I believe that what Mr. Krsnik has before him at the moment is the first demonstrative exhibit, for Hrvatski List, the 18th of November edition. Is that correct? Your Honours, that's OTP Exhibit 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Exhibit 1. Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you stated yesterday that you studied closely this cover page, the text on the cover page of Hrvatski List.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this short shrift -- in fact, can you tell the Trial Chamber what is this text in short shrift on the cover page?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can get a copy of the B/C/S translation of the actual statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the witness is after Exhibit -- what is marked as P11 in the binders. He's after the translation of Van Kuijk's statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Volume 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Exactly, in volume 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you this way -- let us just wait a moment. Let me ask you this way: What is written in short shrift on the cover page of the OTP 1 document, is it -- it is not the transcript from the closed-session testimony of witness Van Kuijk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is correct. It is the excerpts from the witness statement, not the transcripts of the trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A statement that the witness gave to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where he gave that statement and when?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is not shown on the cover page, nor is the date shown on any subsequent page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is indicating the edition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the reference to 1st and 2nd August, 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the reference on the cover -- the front page to "Date of interview: 1st and 2nd, August, 1997"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Cameron, you have the statement with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see the dates Judge Bonomy has referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blocked out in black, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Judges have unredacted, non-redacted version. That may be why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Maybe there is a misunderstanding here, but there is no redacted version. What Judge Bonomy is asking about is very clear, very visible, and visible also in translation on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I was actually referring to the statement itself, which I thought the question related to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the statement itself, it shows the date the 1st and 2nd of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And also in the article it shows the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the blacked-out portion on the lower left-hand corner, it shows the 2nd of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I'm trying to clear up, Your Honours. I want to find out what the document is here and what it constitutes, but I'm trying to do that through the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cameron, have you compared the statement that you have in the Office of the Prosecutor with a document reproduced here in Hrvatski List?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and it's consistent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me how much time passed after that statement when Mr. Van Kuijk testified in closed session?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave the statement in August, and he testified in December of that same year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this statement that he provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, is there any indication of confidentiality or secrecy?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this statement was given to the Office of the Prosecutor, was there a high-ranking officer from the Dutch army present to monitor the provision of the statement?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is not indicated anywhere.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not written anywhere on the record. The statement indicates clearly that Mr. Van Kuijk and the interviewer were alone together with an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I misunderstood the question. During the statement, it was only Mr. Van Kuijk, no one else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about that closed-session testimony? Was it attended by a high-ranking officer from the Dutch army to protect the interests of the Kingdom of the Netherlands for which reason the session was closed in the first place?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a ranking officer in attendance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 7 of the statement given by Mr. Van Kuijk to this Office of the Prosecutor - and I am talking about page 7 of the Croatian statement, in the English version -- it's page 8 in English - it says that Mr. Van Kuijk agreed to testify in public before this Tribunal. Is it written there?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What it says is that -- that "I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I'm repeating a question maybe, but I don't remember your answer. How much time passed after the giving of this statement, the one that was reproduced in the Hrvatski List newspaper when Mr. Van Kuijk testified before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was in August of 1997, and he testified in December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you established whether Hrvatski List ever published the transcript from a closed session?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of any closed session?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] No. No. [Interpretation] No. The transcript from the closed session where Mr. Van Kuijk testified.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question in conclusion, not to take any more of our time. Can you just confirm -- it's the second page in the Croatian version of the statement by Mr. Van Kuijk given to this OTP.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It begins with the third sentence from the bottom of the first paragraph: "I was told that my statement would remain confidential until it is disclosed to the Defence before I am called upon to testify in The Hague."

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the English version it says: "I am requested to make a truthful statement of what I personally saw, heard, or experienced in this connection."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I've been informed by my statement -- that my statement will be kept confidential until it is disclosed to the Defence before I am called upon to testify in The Hague."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course I may not ask you for any conclusions, but doesn't it transpire very clearly from what is written here that he was completely conscious that his testimony would be public, the same as he agreed to testify in a public session before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Graham.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Objection. This is not something that the witness can answer, what Van Kuijk himself thought was the position in relation to the taking of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the statement itself, it would appear that Mr. Van Kuijk was aware that he may be called to call -- testify in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions, but I need to consult with my colleagues briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. Before the Prosecution re-examines the witness, I have one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Certainly. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Cameron, as far as you know, based upon the investigation into this matter, I wonder if you can tell us whether there was any reason by the time of the publication of this very article, that is November 2004, there was any reason for the protective measures to continue. I understand -- I understand Mr. Bralo surrendered before this article was published.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Bralo did -- was surrendered. It's a very difficult question to answer, in a way. The reason for the protective measures, as I understand it, originally were due to circumstances in Bosnia at that particular time. The fact that it had been protected by the court order in the Blaskic case, in my mind, would continue on regardless of the circumstances of the witness. I subsequently spoke to the witness, and by the time that this was published, there was no more personal danger - that's definite - to this witness or to his colleagues. So in that terms, I would agree with Your Honour's supposition that there was no longer any real need for the protective measures, however, the protective measures were still in force at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But from the outset, the reason for personal protection didn't exist. The reason for granting the closed session was because there was sort of sensitivity on the part of the Tribunal and on the part of the Dutch government, not for the reason of personal protection.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for personal protection of Mr. Van Kuijk. According to Mr. Van Kuijk when I spoke to him, his mission in Bosnia was already over. However, his colleagues in the Dutch Battalion were still in Bosnia, and at that particular time Mr. Bralo was still free, and there was a concern that if this information was published, that this could have repercussions upon the Dutch contingent that was still in Bosnia. It was never an issue of personal security for Mr. Van Kuijk himself; it was for his colleagues still in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just one supplementary question. In November 2004, were there Dutch forces in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that reason for protective measures has gone by that stage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Bralo had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that reason -- the secrecy of the indictment reason has gone by then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what reason was there for these protective measures to remain in force in November 2004?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a question I can really answer, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, I think that's a fair comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Graham.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just two points. Re-examined by Ms. Graham:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik identified with you that there was a period of five months between the time when Van Kuijk's statement was taken and when he testified in the Blaskic trial. From your experience as an investigator at the ICTY, are protective measures reassessed in periods of time of that nature?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more point. If you can just have a look at the Hrvatski List edition of the 18th of November, 2004. Have you got that before you?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik drew your attention to the bottom black box, which contains the text, "On 2 August 1997, Dutchman Johannes Van Kuijk stated in his testimony before The Hague Tribunal ..." and you identified that the witness testified in December 1997, not in August.

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your involvement in the investigation in this case, have you got any knowledge of why Hrvatski List might have referred to August as the date of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: TERRANCE CAMERON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It became apparent quite early on that there was -- the word "transcript" was used quite often, and it was confusing as to whether it meant a witness statement or the transcript of testimony. In this particular case, we're dealing here only with the witness statement, which was taken in August, not the court transcripts that were a result of the December. And I should also point out that the part in black is not a part of the official statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GRAHAM
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cameron. That concludes your evidence. Thanks for coming. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, one small matter before we call the witness, which is that last night we contacted the HINA news agency, and I spoke to -- this is in regards to the article of April 27, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. My question is whether you needed Mr. Cameron for that purpose. Let's go --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Well, we have a witness on the witness list who -- who is precisely dedicated to this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, let's hear what you were going to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: However, it's such a small point, I was going to proffer to the Court, and you can decide whether you want to accept it, however, if you want me to have a witness specifically for this particular point, I'm happy to put it on the stand. But we got a letter from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: -- assistant general manager of the HINA news agency, who pulled the article from the archive and provided it to us. It's a fair and accurate -- what we had presented to the Court is a fair and accurate copy of what is in their archive, and he also has a line in his cover letter on the HINA letterhead which explains that where we retrieved it from is a controlled site; it's a compilation of other news services. I can have the witness who contacted the HINA news agency testify to this or I can proffer this to the Court and you can look at it and make a decision whether you want the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was the letter disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We provided it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll hear from the Defence later on, and we'll take a look at the documents, and after hearing from the Defence, we'll make a determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: All right. I will provide this to the usher, who can ... For the record, I would ask that the April 27th article be admitted into evidence based on this information that's being put before the Court, and I know you're going to defer ruling but I just wanted to make that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has been noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: And we will call William Tomljanovich to the stand at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, I wonder whether Defence is in the position to comment on this matter. Can the documents be handed over to the Bench first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence states that this morning we received the letter of Mr. Fjodor Polojac, assistant general manager of the HINA agency, confirming that this is indeed the text of HINA's journalist. So we do not object to that. The source is authentic. However, as for the content, I investigated the matter myself yesterday, and I talked to the author of this text, who absolutely presented his readiness to testify here. He said that this was his free journalistic interpretation in terms of how he, that is to say the journalist, understood this and freely interpreted what was said to him by Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic. These are not the words of Mr. Rebic or Mr. Marijacic but, rather, his free journalistic interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just make one brief comment on what Mr. Krsnik said? I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary. The Chamber is minded to admit this, because there's no issue of authenticity, and it is relevant and has probative value, and the weight -- although the weight is for the Chamber to determine at the later stage, and it is for the Defence to call the author if they so wish it. If they need to. Yes. We will admit the P44 as well as this letter. Could you wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the numbers be given to these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The first exhibit is referenced under P44 and will get the exhibit number OTP 16. While the report -- the letter dated 17th of January will receive the exhibit OTP 17. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the attachment. I think this is a downloaded page from HINA website, official website. Is it true, Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be done. Then let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, with the -- I'm going to ask the Court for a little latitude in order to lead the witness through the preliminary matters, just to get to the heart of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by Mr. Akerson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tomljanovich.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we begin, I just wanted to re-advise you that you're going to be talking about documents that concern not only Mr. Van Kuijk, whose protection has been lifted, but other witnesses where protections still remain. So if you encounter a witness who you think might be protected, please just refer to that person as "protected witness."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And secondly, we are going to be showing documents electronically. If I could just make sure they're not going to be distributed outside the courtroom, published outside the courtroom. Thank you very much. Mr. Tomljanovich, I'm just going to run through some of your educational --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a Ph.D. from Yale University?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In history; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: In history, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, and you wrote your thesis on a subject that is related to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, 19th century Croatian history, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are very familiar with Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked not to overlap each other and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you can read the transcript, you are being asked to -- not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And to put a pause between questions and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to talk about -- sorry. Let me move -- let me just ask you: When did you begin work at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: March 2nd, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what has been your position at the Tribunal since you started?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I've been a research officer in the leadership research team of the investigations division of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that position, what has been your primary responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, primarily, the people in our office are all people who can read B/C/S and have an advanced degree -- something having to do with the former Yugoslavia, and we spend most of our time dealing with political structures in the former Yugoslavia and analysing political structures and dealing very heavily, of course, with documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And we're going to talk about two kinds of documents today; documents that the OTP obtained from Croatian archives and also transcripts from meetings in the Croatian Presidency. What has been your assignment in regards to these two kinds of documents specifically?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, first of all, with the documents obtained from the Croatian archives, I've been working extensively with those documents since they were made available to us, or large numbers of them were made available to us beginning in April of 2000. I went on many of the missions to review and copy archival documents, organise some of those missions, analyse those documents and process those documents when they came up to The Hague. Now, with the presidential transcripts, it's the same thing. I reviewed those beginning in May of 2000, took also part in some of the requests for additional transcripts, reviewed the lists of transcripts, and I worked for about one year indexing and cataloguing the collection of transcripts we have in house from the Presidency of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to -- before we get into the subject of the first document that we're going to be talking about, which is a transcript of a meeting in the Croatian Presidency, I wanted to have the -- hand to the usher for the Court a demonstrative aid, but if you can put on the first Sanction exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note Mr. Krsnik is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't know. I have to ask you. Please instruct me, because I don't know what direction this examination is taking. I see that transcripts from meetings in the Croatian Presidency are being referred to. May I ask what this has to do with the indictment due to which we are here today, and what does it have to do with the indictment that we are discussing here today? The office of the president of the Republic of Croatia and these transcripts, what does this have to do with my client Mr. Rebic, and Mr. Marijacic? Please, let us not move beyond the scope of the indictment. Let's deal with what the indictment says. Please let us not go beyond that. Honestly, I don't know what this has to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Akerson can clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I can. I'm understanding that objection is an objection to the relevance of this material, and there's three points that these documents are relevant to. First, there's an issue that the 2000 order deals with publication, that there's a prohibition against publication of material, and in particular this first document that you're going to be receiving into evidence has a transcript of a meeting where Mr. Rebic is sitting with two newspapers with a specific intent of taking a document leaked from the OTP to have it published. One of the issues raised by the Defence is the meeting where they discussed the protected material. This will be clear evidence on the intent of Mr. Rebic that this material he provided to Hrvatski List was going to be published, because he's been doing so since 1997. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, what is this, some kind of similar fact evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think it's -- it shows a pattern of behaviour and clear evidence of knowledge and motive. Taken in conjunction with the other documents that we're going to show in which it's on Mr. Rebic's letterhead, signed by Mr. Rebic and/or somebody who was directly subordinated to him where he is distributing ICTY protected material, clearly demonstrating that he knows it's protected information, and he's advising others on the nature of those protections, including the specifics of those protections, down to the ID of the witnesses protected and the content of the information that he's protected -- that he's submitting is protected. So it goes to his understanding of the protections that are in order. It's clearly relevant to what we have to prove against -- of his knowledge in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson. We'll hear from Mr. Ivanovic first. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you turn on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to draw your attention to a mistake that the OTP is making. The Hrvatski List did not exist in 1997, so Mr. Rebic at that time certainly could not have made a decision to publish something or not to publish something in Hrvatski List. As for the rest, Mr. Krsnik is going to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Office of the Prosecutor will not object when I say that Hrvatski List came into existence in 2004. Secondly, what Mr. Prosecutor said, this is not true in terms of what I read, but we'll deal with the transcripts later. But this happened before 2000. This is a discussion from 1997. And what you said to this Honourable Trial Chamber is that you invoked the year 2000 and you said that that is when it existed, when it did not exist, and I don't see the relevance of this conversation and what it has to do with Hrvatski List, and also publishing Mr. Van Kuijk's statement, which is what my client -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can -- if I can respond, just one quick point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The underlying case where the protections emanate is the Blaskic case. All the documents that -- that -- all the evidence that I'm going to adduce all concern the Blaskic case and the dissemination of protected materials in the Blaskic case. It's directly relevant to the orders that were in -- that would apply in 1997, 1998, when all of these communications were made. And lastly, the evidence will show the extent of the communication that Mr. Rebic had with the Blaskic Defence team, which would tend to prove that it would be more likely that he would have known about the 2000 order, which is one of the things that we're specifically required to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, do you have anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to draw your attention to a fact. The document that was submitted in the Prosecution documents from the president's office is the 7th of May, 1997. The protective measures orders -- order issued in the Blaskic case was issued on the 6th of June, 1997, so all of this happened beforehand, it had nothing to do with it, not even indirectly. I wish to recall the Appeals Chamber ruling of the 26th of January, 2006 [as interpreted] where it decided on the foundation for the protective measures from 1996. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will grant the Prosecution to lead the evidence, considering that it may be related to the pattern of conduct, the state of his mind, though marginally related, but the weight for it is for the Chamber to determine, and there I thank the Defence for their comment on this matter. That has been noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I would just like to ask if the demonstrative aid has been -- demonstrative exhibit has been distributed to the Court. I have copies for the Defence as well. And if it could be put up electronically on Sanction but not distributed -- that this would not be distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, before we get into the presidential transcript, we're going to be talking about, in these documents, names of people and I wanted to give the Court a very, very simple idea of the relationship between the people's names. Do you see a document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's diagram of the relationship between a few people's names in the Croatian government that are relevant to your examination today. Can you just confirm -- can you just, in a couple of sentences, describe who these people are and their relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'd like to ask whether Defence is all right with the last name being shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment, Your Honour? I think I can address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, in just a couple of sentences, describe who these people are and why they're related in this diagram.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, first of all I should point out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I should point out on this -- this is an overly -- or a very simplified chart here. It doesn't show the structure of the Croatian intelligence agencies as such, which are -- is there a problem? It doesn't show the structure of the agencies, because there's about a half dozen large agencies. This just shows the reporting that goes on in some of the documents which we'll be talking about today. At the -- I'll go from the bottom to the top. At the bottom, we have the security and information service, the SIS, which was the military counter-intelligence agency of the Republic of Croatia, established in 1991. And for most of the period we're going to talk about today, in the late 1990s, Ante Gugic was the chief of that agency. His immediate superior was the assistant minister of defence for intelligence and security affairs, which is Markica Rebic. Above him is the minister of defence, to whom he reports, who for most of this period, until his death in May of 1998, was Gojko Susak, who was succeeded by Andrija Hebrang and General Miljevac. And above him in the reporting chain that we see in the correspondence we're looking at today is the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman. Off to the side, some of this material is also sent to Miroslav Tudjman who was, during most of this period until the spring of 1998 and then again for part of 1999, the chief of the Croatian reporting service, which was the foreign intelligence agency of the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Miroslav Tudjman is the son of President Franjo Tudjman. And he's not in the same -- he's not connected with this same chain of subordination in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while communication probably generally followed this line of communication, are there exceptions where individuals in this chain of command also communicated directly to people above or below them not in this clear chain of command?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on now to the transcripts of the Croatian Presidency. We're going to be presenting one document to Your Honours today. Mr. Tomljanovich, how did -- how did it come to be that meetings in the Presidency of Croatia were recorded and transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, I think Judge Robinson may remember this from the Kordic trial: President Franjo Tudjman recorded some of his meetings in his own office and elsewhere, beginning at least in 1991 and continuing until his death in 1999. That was done by staff of his own office, two of whom testified, I think it was in closed session, or at least with protection for their names, in the Kordic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm happy that the witness reminded Judge Robinson of the matter of transcripts. The transcripts never received official authorisation nor did we have them in the official documentation of this Tribunal. The transcripts were never included in the trial or the judgement in Kordic case. Until this day, this Tribunal never accepted transcripts or accepted their authenticity. Many witnesses have been questioned to this issue, and it was established many times the transcripts have no basis, either in video material or audio material or CDs. Croatian courts made their decision, rather, a series of decisions, maintaining that they're not authentic, and the Croatian law from 1999 under one minister, and then under another minister in 2000, sealed the transcripts for 30 years so that they would not be manipulated precisely because their authenticity has not been established, and that was my main, primary reason. We will be discussing transcripts here and dealing in high level policies whereas my client was charged with Novi List -- rather, Hrvatski List. Look at what we are discussing here: The structures of a state whereas President Tudjman, as you know, has been dead for six years. Mr. Susak has been dead for seven years, et cetera. We are now listening to a professional investigator of the OTP who will now be lecturing us on the subject, and after that I will have to cross-examine for God knows how long because I will have to go through all these questions. Listening to what he's saying, I will of course have to cross-examine at length, then call witnesses I hadn't intended to call, and then call witnesses who attended the meetings - those who are alive, at least - to see -- to try to prove my point about the transcripts. Thank you for hearing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your opposition is mainly related to the admission of transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Because, Your Honour, that would really force me to call witnesses to deal with it, because those transcripts have never proven to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say they were rejected in Kordic? You say the transcripts were rejected in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. As far as I remember, towards the end of debate in Kordic, the Prosecution tried, towards the end of the trial, to introduce transcripts, to have them admitted, but Judge -- late Judge May refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The purpose for which their admission is being sought today is not the same as the purpose for which their admission was being sought in Kordic. We'll have to consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can respond. I -- Defence counsel is of course obligated to attack the -- I mean, one of the things that he could choose to attack on cross-examination is the credibility of these transcripts. This witness will -- he can testify to the reason, I think, that the transcripts were not admitted in Kordic, which don't relate, in my understanding, to their authenticity or their credibility. It was a different reason. But I'm going to lay the foundation and he's free to try to establish that they are not authentic, and the Court can give them whatever weight they want. I don't think this deals with the admissibility, which has already been ruled upon. What Mr. Krsnik is raising are questions of the weight of the evidence, and that has to be determined by you at the end of this trial, but I think, you know, we need to move on and just get this into evidence and you can give it whatever weight you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Tomljanovich -- Mr. Tomljanovich can give evidence as to how the OTP got in possession of those documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That's -- that's the next question. I was just talking to him about the process by which these were transcribed and then I have a series of questions related to the reliability of these transcripts. I think Mr. Tomljanovich can even talk a little bit about the Kordic trial because he's been involved in these transcripts for six years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He's not in the position to give evidence as to the very authenticity of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No, he is. He -- we relied on them because we had to form a basis in the OTP that they were reliable documents, and so we've done that through various means. And when you hear that evidence, then it's -- then you can give that whatever weight you want and it can be -- it can be challenged on cross-examination and then on the totality of the evidence, you can determine what weight you want to give these. But it's our position that they are true and accurate copies of transcripts that were made of meetings. They represent what was actually said in the meetings, and they are authentic and should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted, Mr. Krsnik, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am trying to be guided by common sense, as Judge Bonomy advised. I have been reckoning that this trial would be flexible, but if we go on with attempts to prove various points this way, then the Defence will have to change its position and call a much greater number of witnesses. If we try to stick to our previous resolution and treat this as simple, straightforward, we could maintain our -- our previous decision. But if the Prosecution goes on this way ...

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: If I could just make one other comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will allow the Prosecution to lead the evidence. However, we'll determine the admissibility of that transcript after having heard the cross-examination from the Defence. But I would like the parties to move on expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'll get through this very quickly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, how many of the presidential transcripts does the OTP have in its general collection?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, the number is exactly 666.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of these transcripts have you personally reviewed and analysed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: All of them. And if I could, I would like to add one thing about Mr. Krsnik's comment just a minute ago about the admissibility of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why not just answer the questions you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just answer the questions. That may come up in cross-examination, but let's just move on.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your knowledge of these transcripts, what was the process by which they were made in President Tudjman's office?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: President Tudjman's staff placed microphones in two rooms in the Presidency; one room next to his office and another larger conference room. That was connected to recording machinery. The stenographers were in a separate room, listening to the tapes, and as the tapes were being made, the stenographers were making stenographic transcripts of the meetings as they went along. This would be checked against the tapes and then it would be filed in the archive of the Presidency. In some cases, meetings were taped which were not on the premises of the -- of the Presidency. In that case, tapes were made remotely and then brought back to the stenographers of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know about this process?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: From having -- well, both proofed and listened to the testimony of the persons who actually made these transcripts in the Kordic trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they professional transcribers, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. One of them was one of the women who was transcribing the documents, the other was the gentleman who actually took care of the recording equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the transcribers checked the accuracy of their transcription against the recording, what -- against the audio tape of the recording, what did they do with that tape?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: You mean over the long run.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the long run.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yeah. Generally speaking, once the transcripts had been made, they would tape over the cassette tapes they were using. Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the final product of the transcription was the physical paper transcript?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which had been transcribed by a professional stenographer, checked against an audio recording, and then filed in an archive?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how has the OTP been able to check or assess that these are accurate transcripts of these meetings? In other words, are there secondary sources of the content of these meetings which can be compared against the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, yes, as a matter of fact. With a collection of this size and of this breadth, you have to imagine not only it's 600-odd transcripts we have in our possession, some of these meetings are quite long, go on for many hours, and involve sometimes dozens of participants. So the amount of detail and references to events outside of the transcripts is very great, and all of that can be checked against the transcripts. Furthermore, individuals who took part in those meetings have authenticated the transcripts, and beyond that, in some instances individuals who were at the meetings taking notes, we've had access to their notes, which match the transcripts as well. And on some occasions with some of the later transcripts, the audio recordings do survive, and we've checked a number of audio recordings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just advise you, I think only one of your microphones is turned on. If you could turn on the other microphone.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk about -- without using the name -- without mentioning the name of the witness that we had discussed in our proofing session, there was a witness who took copious notes of meetings. Can you tell the Court about that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Am I not allowed to mention his name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't mention his name. Don't give any more descriptive information.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, an American diplomat who has testified in a number of cases here and took copious notes of all his meetings, and I've had the opportunity to check his notes against the meetings he was present in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did they compare with the transcript of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Very well. His note taking was really outstanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they -- his notes of the meeting corroborated the accuracy of the transcript of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving on to the audiotapes, how many audiotapes did survive from this transcription process?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: That I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many are in our possession?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I believe four or five are in our possession. In the archive of the Presidency, there's quite a few more audiotapes, but I haven't listened to those and they're not in our possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the audiotapes that are in the possession of the OTP, have you reviewed the audio and compared it to the transcripts to verify the transcripts are true and accurate copies of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about the content of these transcripts? I want to ask you, because you've reviewed so many of these transcripts, over 600, does the content of these transcripts themselves -- or itself, suggest that these are fair and accurate transcripts of the meetings --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- which they record? Okay. And so you're confident that the transcripts of the presidential meetings that you've reviewed are true and accurate transcripts of the meetings they record?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'd like to present the witness with a document that's been previously marked as Prosecution Exhibit 7, and I'm providing to him both the English and the B/C/S versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, may I just ask the witness as a matter of fact, which may not necessarily be determinative of the issue here, were the transcripts admitted in Kordic? Because I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only submitted one transcript during the Prosecution case. That transcript was admitted. We then came into possession of additional transcripts later, and I'm not entirely sure looking back on it, but I think the issue was the fairness and the late submission of -- and I believe as well Judge May mentioned redundancy as an issue with those transcripts, which came in very late. And if I may, I could also -- I'd also like to comment on the admission in the Tuta/Stela trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Not now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll have the matter checked anyhow. Yes, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, do you have two documents in front of you that are marked as Prosecution Exhibit 7 and 7/E, which is the translation of those documents?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you identify those documents for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is the minutes of a working meeting held in Franjo Tudjman's office on the 7th of May, 1997, at 6.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: 7th of May, 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask that this document be put up electronically in Sanction. And I just want to advise you again that this meeting concerns a protected witness still in the Blaskic case, so do not mention him by name.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document should not be broadcast outside the courtroom. Who are the participants in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, the participants in this meeting are President Tudjman himself; Nenad Ivankovic, who was an editor at the daily paper Vjesnik at the time; Gojko Susak, who was the minister of defence at the time; Branko Tudjen, who was an editor at Vecernji List, which is a daily tabloid in Zagreb; Markica Rebic, who was assistant minister of defence at the time; and I believe as well Mr. Goran Radin appears, but just briefly, in the transcript. He's one of the president's advisors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there's two newspapers in this meeting; Vecernji List and Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the -- what is the nature of this meeting? What are they discussing?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: They're -- the persons in this meeting have in their possession a witness statement which was given to the OTP by the particular protected witness whose name we see here, and most of the discussion in this meeting is about the statement itself as well about -- as well as to when they should release it to the newspapers and how they should release it to the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Mr. Rebic participating in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, actively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you go to page 3, the English transcript, and explain to the Court what this particular passage or section of the transcript is referring to.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: They're discussing how they're going to publish this. Mr. Ivankovic says that there will be need for an introduction, and the president says that the Blaskic Defence team got the document. And then on the next page -- on the video we don't have that page up. Thank you. Or do we? Yes. Mr. Rebic then says that he's spoken to the Defence attorney Nobilo and that he's not against this. Quite on the contrary, he says it would be good to publish this statement but that they can't mention that he gave it to them because that would be a violation of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Rebic is expressing concern that the document is protected and it could expose Mr. Nobilo to liability.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a slight discrepancy in the translation. In English it says [In English] "Confidential" [Interpretation] whereas in Croatian we read something quite different. Maybe it's similar, but it is different, and it's extremely illiterate, ungrammatical, as all transcripts are, and it's very difficult to follow them. But we'll deal with it in cross-examination. The English version is much nicer, reads much better than the Croatian original. The literal translation is that Mr. Nobilo has nothing against it. On the contrary, he also says it would be good to publish it, but it should not be quoted that he had provided it because he had to support confidentiality, discretion. That's what we read if we see -- if we translate literally the Croatian text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thanks for the clarification. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that if Defence counsel has a question about any translation, he can ask the Court interpreters to read the B/C/S version of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the problem arose because the witness paraphrased the content of the transcript. If he had read the transcript, then there wouldn't have been an issue, because the word "advocate" appears in the transcript in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I will address this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read this passage in the B/C/S form --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Or, Your Honours, can I have the court interpreters translate this? I can put the B/C/S version on the screen and we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point's resolved. We can move on to something else that might be relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the next passage here, Mr. Tomljanovich?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: The next passage after Mr. Rebic's comment. They then discuss -- would you like me to read it or would you like me to paraphrase it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead and read it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Okay. Then Mr. Rebic says: "I would present it like this. I mean --" well, no, I'm sorry. I'll start with President Tudjman then. President Tudjman says: "Then it should be said that he went in and that he did that within the process against Blaskic." And then Mr. Rebic says: "I would present it like this. I mean, I don't know. I would give it as a proposal. I would make a series of articles of that. First that it -- what would appear would -- first what would appear would be the commentary on the first page in Vjesnik, like it is in the source --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not written anywhere "a series of articles."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian original never mentions what we are hearing from the witness in the English version. I can read to you, with the help of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the witness able to read the B/C/S? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like me to read the same passage from Mr. Rebic here in the B/C/S original out loud?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. This is Markica Rebic. [Interpretation] I don't know whether I would make it as a proposal. I would make a sausage out of it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Full stop. Full stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First -- the first thing that would come out would be a comment on the cover page of Vjesnik, something like this: From sources close to the ICTY through our observers, news was received, or obtained, and then only the basic contents would be indicated. Full stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask a question now that -- the English translation that the Court has in front of it indicates that the B/C/S passage says series of articles.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The court interpreters have interpreted that as "sausage."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on the discrepancy between those two?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, I imagine that when Mr. Rebic was talking about making a sausage, he was speaking figuratively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to -- the witness should -- sorry. The witness's job is to translate. The witness's job is not to comment, in answer to that question, on what was intended by the comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear that in mind, Mr. Tomljanovich.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on, Mr. Akerson. We will have three minutes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I, before you move on, ask a question. Do all of these articles relate to the same protected witness in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'm now going to present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: -- to the witness what has been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 9, and 9B, which is in Your Honours' first binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which has been already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: It's admitted as OTP Exhibit ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, I'm showing you an order from the Blaskic trial. And if Your Honours could look at the next slide. If you can put the next slide in Sanction up on the screen. This is a passage from that order, and can you confirm that the two newspapers referred to in the Blaskic order are the same newspapers that had participated in -- as -- with the editors of those newspapers in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes; Vecernji List and Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to the next document. These are documents from the Croatian archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, whether this is appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That's fine, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, for you to continue your examination. However, given the short period of time scheduled to take place for this trial, we have to focus on the main points. Please move on very expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: All right, Your Honours. I'm just going to lead for a very short period of time to get through the preliminary matters regarding documents from the Croatian archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, the OTP went in missions -- in three waves of missions to review large collections of documents that were contained in Croatian governmental archives in 2000, 2004, 2005; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, yes. Actually, there were more waves of missions than that, but there's three that are relevant to us, I think, today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you participated materially in those missions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. The ones in 2004 and 2005, I organised myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many missions have you gone on to inspect documents, governmental documents, in Croatia, can you estimate for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Quite a few times. I haven't been keeping count, but about a dozen times in the last five years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2000, the documents principally reviewed and analysed were a large collection of HVO documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. In mid-2000, we received access to the large collection of HVO documentation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I please ask the Trial Chamber to react now. Now we've touched upon the HVO, which is the army of another state, Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the Trial Chamber undoubtedly knows. Are we going to allow that topic too? If you think it is inappropriate to start discussing it now, could you please rule accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we not wait until -- until we hear what it is about? Please go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in 2000, you go down, inspect a lot of documents that are in this large collection, largely of HVO documents. September of 2004, you go and inspect a different collection. What collection of documents is that principally?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: At the end of 2000, we were assured by the authorities in Croatia that all -- that all materials coming from -- that all materials in their possession from the HVO had been placed in the state archives. In mid-2004, it came to our attention that there was another collection of documents in the Republic of Croatia which we had not yet seen. We made it -- we were not sure initially if these documents were copies of documents we'd already seen or if these were actual materials that were new to us. We discovered, after having obtained access to them in the summer of 2004, that a great deal of this material was in fact new to us and very relevant to appeals which were then pending.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me intervene because the main point I want to make here is this is a different collection. You went on a number of missions to review a number of documents; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of those collections included a collection of documents caught the Blaskic collection. That was 94 binders of material including evidence from the Blaskic trial?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. That was the -- this is the material I'm discussing just a minute ago. There were a number of collections within that group of documents. One group was called Tihomir Blaskic documents. Another group of documents was called documents originating from or copied by Dario Kordic. Another collection, subcollection in this larger collection, was documents of the HVO which had been used as attachments in reports of the Republic of Croatia SIS. And there was also a couple of other smaller collections which aren't of any particular interest except for videos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2005, a six-person team went down to analyse documents of about 112 binders of material in the third main mission to inspect these Croatian documents. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. That was a follow-up to this first mission, and I believe it was seven persons. I include myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You go to Croatia. You are reviewing documents in an archive. When you find a document that appears to have evidentiary value, you execute a form, you receive a copy, and that copy that you receive from the archivist in Croatia is then verified by you or the OTP staff member that it's an accurate copy of what's in the archive; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. The specifics of how we operate in different sites may be slightly different, but we always confirm the copies are what we ordered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And once the copy is obtained from us, we -- the OTP's process would be to transport it to its evidence vault here in The Hague, either by courier or by diplomatic pouch; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. Generally speaking, yes, although I should add that from 2000 -- late 2000 until early 2004 some documents were initially processed in the field office in Zagreb and then eventually sent up to the vault by the means you indicated, but that was because of the volume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The documents that we're going to be seeing today, do they -- are you familiar with all of these documents?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are they fair and accurate copies of documents that were in the Croatian archives at the time that the OTP had identified them as having evidentiary value?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the specific documents. Before I present a document to you -- before I present the first document to you, were there documents in this collection that involved Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the agency that he was in charge of, the SIS?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did these documents refer to specific operations that -- that the SIS was involved with, the Blaskic trial?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, yes. And not only the Blaskic trial but all of the cases here at the ICTY in which Croat defendants were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The operations I'm referring to are OA Haag, OA Istina, OA Put, OA Arhiv. Can you tell the Court what these operations are?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, you've mentioned a few different ones here. For the most part, these are operations involving mainly the Croatian secret police authorities, designed to assist the Defence of indicted Croats at the ICTY. That would be the case for OA Haag, and OA Put, and also OA Proces, and also in later times OA Sigma. OA Arhiv was a separate operation designed to move, or intending to move archival materials from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatian army barracks in Borongaj in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik is on his feet. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want to put a completely different question, so could you please clarify this: Could you please ask the witness, on the basis of what we know and what we saw, all these documents are marked strictly confidential, military secret. It is highly secretive, the highest level of confidentiality. I cannot allow myself to be criminally responsible once I go back to my country. When I come back, the Croatian authorities are going to say, "Why did you not stop the confidential materials of the Croatian state being exposed in public session?" There are no representatives here of the Croatian state - I don't know why - but can this be stated in public? You may recall that the government of the Republic of Croatia before this Court won its case in the subpoena duces tecum proceedings when this Court in its judgement exactly specified which documents can be sought and indeed received and discussed. That was the Chamber that was presided over by the former President of the Tribunal, Gabrielle Kirk McDonald. And I would really like to know whether there is no longer a sign of confidentiality on these documents. Is there a relevant decision to that effect taken by the Croatian government? So can this be discussed in public? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought we would come to the issue very soon, but, Mr. Akerson, could you clarify this matter, whether these matters can be discussed in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The documents that I'm about to present should not be broadcast but not for the reasons that Mr. Krsnik is explaining. They shouldn't be broadcast because they pertain to the protected witnesses still in the Blaskic trial. These documents that are in our possession were turned over by the Croatian authorities pursuant to their treaty agreement with us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without any conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These are documents that are available for use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to present two documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not a person who is easily frightened, and I've been an attorney-at-law for the past 25 years, thank God. So when a document says defence, military secret, strictly confidential, according to our laws is the highest degree of protection. I would like to see a document issued by the Croatian government giving approval for these documents to be discussed in public. Imagine this kind of thing happening in America. Imagine if a document marked this way would be presented before a court of law in the States. I really wonder what would happen to my colleague in that case if he did not have government approval to disclose this kind of document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask, Mr. Krsnik, whether you are making this opposition on behalf of the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, indeed not, Your Honour. I just don't want to expose myself to possible prosecution in my own country once I get off the plane. Of course this is not premeditated in any way, and there is no intent on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we heard from the Prosecution in express term that they received a clear go from the Croatian government. So it is the Prosecution's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. In that case, in Croatia, criminal proceedings will be instituted against the Prosecutor if he did not have approval from the Croatian government. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, the Prosecutor is an officer of this court and we must accept his word that he received approval from the Croatian government without any conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
