utterances.text: If I could have the usher present to the witness a document which has been previously marked as Prosecution Exhibit 16, which I believe is in binder 2 document -- of your documents. And if you could put that electronically on the screen. Just the English version on the screen, please. Mr. Tomljanovich, we're going to move through these documents pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you identify this document, please, by first starting with the date, author, and recipient.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This document was written on the 24th of December, 1997, and it's signed by Ante Gugic, who at the time was a director of the SIS, on behalf of his immediate superior, Assistant Minister Brigadier Markica Rebic, and it's being sent to the minister of defence, Gojko Susak, and the head of the Croatian Information Service, Miroslav Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to remind you that this document contains the name of a witness who is protected and you shouldn't mention the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How and when did this document come into the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is one of the documents we reviewed on this mission in January 2005. It was in a binder which was given to us by representatives of the Ministry of Defence, the Republic of Croatia. We ordered the copy through the Office for Cooperation for -- with the ICTY, and the copy was delivered to the Zagreb field office of the ICTY on 21st of February, 2005.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this -- sorry. Is this document a fair and accurate copy of the document that was in the Croatian archive?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to remind the Court, Mr. Gugic is a direct subordinate of Mr. Rebic, and he is sending this letter on Mr. Rebic's behalf?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: He was in December of 1997, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court the purpose of this letter? Why don't you read the passage instead of explaining. Why don't you read this passage that's highlighted there in the document before you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Before I read the passage that's highlighted, I'll mention first that it's a cover letter which accompanies closed-session testimony from the Blaskic trial, and then in the highlighted portion, it reads: "The witness in this case is a protected witness according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY, and in this way, his name and the content of his testimony are protected from public knowledge, so that the release of any part of the attachment of this memorandum would constitute a grave violation of international law."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to go to the next document now, which has been previously marked as Prosecution Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to tender all these documents at one time rather than making individual tenders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: And can the electronic version of this document be put on screen if it's not already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, do you have in front of you a document that is identified as Prosecution Exhibit 17?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you identify this document starting with the author and the intended recipient and the date?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is a letter from Assistant Minister Staff Brigadier Markica Rebic, signed and stamped, to the director of the Croatian Information Service, Miroslav Tudjman, and the date is 11th of February, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this letter is on the official letterhead of Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. It's the letterhead of his office, the office of the assistant minister for security, and it has the serial number corresponding to that office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it contains a signature and a stamp and office, an official office stamp?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this letter occurs after the exhibit that we just discussed and references that exhibit, which is Prosecution Exhibit 16?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, it does. On -- I guess it's third line in both the original and the translation, the date and serial number of that previous letter is cited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please go down to what is the last paragraph in this letter and read what Mr. Rebic at that time is advising Miroslav Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without revealing the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "... a protected witness, is a protected witness according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY, and in this way, the name and content of his testimony are protected from public knowledge, so that the release of any part of the attachment of this memorandum would constitute a grave violation of international law."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This document, is it a fair and accurate copy of the document that you analysed in the Croatian archive?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and I should add that the redaction in the original -- or in the copy we have here, in the B/C/S original, was made by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia before we reviewed the material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you know that, the redaction was done by the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We were told -- well, in particular, when we were reviewed these materials, we were informed of the redactions which were made by various agencies. In the case of the Ministry of Defence, when we received the copies of these documents, we -- they also included -- and this was only the Ministry of Defence, the other agencies did not do this -- they provided us with an accompanying document which explained why they'd redacted what they'd redacted. Usually making -- usually they invoked, I believe -- I don't know the rules that well, I'm not a lawyer, but I think it was Rule 54 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a pending request for assistance in order to get the unredacted version of this document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. Of the documents that we obtained copies of last February, we've also made an additional follow-up request to receive unredacted copies of roughly a hundred documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the OTP has not received the unredacted copy of these documents as of yet?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to now present what's been previously marked as Prosecution Exhibit 18 and 18/E, also in Exhibit 2 of Your Honours' binders, I believe. Once again I'll advise you you don't want to mention any witness names in these documents.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they should not be broadcast outside of the courtroom. The document is electronically available on the courtroom screens. Can you identify this document which is marked as Exhibit 18, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This document comes from a redacted author who's writing using the ID number and letterhead of the office of the assistant minister for security of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and he's writing to a redacted addressee, and it -- but it is also stamped for receipt by the HIS. And the date of the document is 17th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I apologise to the Honourable Trial Chamber, but I'm so tired of getting up all the time. It's not true again. In the Croatian original, it says very clearly who received the report. The report was received by the office for national security. This is a completely different agency. Of course, I will have the time and honour to discuss this during the cross-examination. So it is the national security office that received this, and now does the witness know that the HIS is part of that service? That is something that we will discuss when our time comes, but that's not it. Thank you for this intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In Croatian version there is no abbreviation of HIS, as was noted by an English translation. That has been noted. Thank you. Please go on, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to point out, the redactions in this document, were they also done by the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, although this particular document, which we got on the same mission, was provided to us by the intelligence agency, or OA is the is the acronym for them, and they are the successor to the HIS, which is discontinued. And as a rule, they were more liberal with -- or less liberal, depending how you look at it, with the redactions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point being that the redactions were done by the Croatian government. We've requested an unredacted document and we have not received that unredacted document as of yet.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, what is the nature of this document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: The author is alerting the addressee that a protected witness has begun testifying in the case against Tihomir Blaskic, and it names that witness by name, and they inform the HIS that they will keep them informed of this protected witness's testimony, and a similar warning to the ones we've seen before is at the bottom of the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The letter references a summary of the closed-session testimony of the protected witness as being delivered by this letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: With this particular document, unlike the other two, I don't see an attachment, but I might not be looking in the right place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. If you can look at the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and just read that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Read that second paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I'll read the second paragraph. It is there. It wasn't highlighted. "According to the source's prediction, the testimony of" this protected witness -- and in the original the protected witness is named, of course. When I say "protected witness," they're using his name. "... and his cross-examination will last three days (until 18 March 1998).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The date of this letter is the day after this witness's testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a day after the protected witness testifies at the ICTY, this letter, which emanates from Mr. Rebic's office, is circulated, containing the content -- a summary of the content of the protected witness's statement?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, I believe we must not allow this, and I object to any conclusions being drawn. The witness cannot draw his conclusions here. It is not written anywhere in this document who sent it to inform whom or that it is from the office of Mr. Rebic. That is a conclusion of the witness. The bureau or office for security does not mean it is Mr. Rebic's office. Mr. Rebic was at the head of the whole sector in the Ministry of Defence and had many people under him. But that is -- what was said was a conclusion made by the witness, and I don't think it actually follows from what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: If I can respond, Your Honour. We never said that this came personally from Mr. Rebic but from his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'll move on to the next document, which is Prosecution ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, the Chamber finds your question where you said, The day after the protected witness testifies at the ICTY, this letter which emanates from Mr. Rebic's office is circulated concerning the content," et cetera, leading. So -- and the conclusion of the matter is for the Chamber to determine later on. So could you bear that in mind? So the Chamber is minded to sustain the opposition in relation to this matter. Or could you reformulate the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, is it okay for you to mention the content of the protected witness's evidence, whether we can identify the witness or not? Think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Referring back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Robinson has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, I'm beginning to become more than a little concerned about this line of examination. Are you really asking the Chamber to draw an inference of guilt from this evidence of previous conduct in relation to the particular charges which relates to a later date and event? Is this what you're really doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The purpose of this evidence is to show Mr. Rebic's understanding of the protections that are in place, and the article that was published in Hrvatski List on November 18th, 2004, what is explicitly admitted is that protections apply but there's no discussion as to what specific -- what specifically is protected. This evidence clearly shows that Mr. Rebic had a knowledge of not only the protection supplied but what those protections were. This is not evidence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But how could it show that he would know what the protections were in relation to the specific matter before the Court now?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: It demonstrates that he has a knowledge that witness protection includes identity and content and, therefore, on November 18th in 2004, if there was a question, he knows that there are these two components to protections, and he's responsible for then ascertaining before he participates in the publication of what is known as protected material to find out whether or not it's protected as to identity or content, but it demonstrates clearly a very detailed knowledge of the kinds of protection that apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think that would be a fair inference to draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's more to it than that. The order affecting these witnesses would no doubt be a different order from the one that we're considering. They're witnesses who give evidence in closed session, so one would need to look at the closed session background decision, which we're not here to do. We're not here to explore other cases. I, at the moment, can draw no inferences from any of this evidence, I make it clear to you. And if it's all of the same pattern, then it's pointless hearing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the key issue here that has to be cleared up before this witness continues is whether any of the statements mentioned here was published by 1999 until when Mr. Rebic had effective control, whether the allegation made by the Prosecutor could be relevant. If it was published after 1999, it's a different matter, and it has nothing to do with the testimony of Van Kuijk or Hrvatski List, because none of these documents mention either Hrvatski List or Mr. Marijacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That actually is a separate point, which highlights further the potential irrelevancy of this evidence, because the things that are being done here are things that it is understandable for an agent in the security service to be doing in the interest of his state. Whether it's justified or not is another matter, but understandable. And it's quite different conduct from giving something to a journalist. Now, you've not suggested that you're using it to indicate that he would give something to a journalist for publication, so it may be that what Mr. Ivanovic says forms no part of the case. But if you are going to suggest that, then I again would find it impossible, on what we've seen so far, to draw the inference from what's going on behind the scenes, telling people explicitly that this is to be kept private within our own confines as indicative at all as an intent to publish material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, does this evidence go on in the same vein for some time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: There's one additional document and then I'm done --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: -- on these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the transcript relates to events in 1997, seven years before what we're talking about, in a clearly political situation, quite different from the sort of situation that this case is about, and the others relate to protected witnesses in respect of whom the orders might be different from the order in the present case, or might have been made for different reasons from the order in the present case.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think what these documents show is that Mr. Rebic was in possession of the knowledge that this -- the protections were closed-session orders. What we have in 2004 is Mr. Rebic providing a transcript that clearly indicates this is closed-session testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But am I right in saying that the reasons for closed-session testimony in the two cases we've had so far may well be different? In fact, are obviously going to be different from the reasons behind the closed-session testimony in the present case.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Very likely that there are going to be differences. However, what it does show is that Mr. Rebic knew that there were these different components of closed-session protection. Because one of his arguments can be that I knew some protections applied but I didn't have the specifics so you can't hold me responsible for violating protections which I only knew of generally, and this very clearly establishes beyond a reasonable doubt that he knew the specifics of what protections could apply to a witness. At that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: At that point, he's responsible if he's going to publish -- to make the call to the Tribunal to ascertain what those protections are before he goes ahead and publishes. There are occasions where you can't publish the content of a witness's testimony but you're free to say that he testified at the Tribunal. You have to know that there's a difference between an identity being protected or not and the content of what he testifies to being protected or not. And I would like to address as long as -- I mean, it seems like the Court would like a proffer on the relevance of the transcript of the presidential meeting, and I'm happy to make that, because what it shows, which I would have tied up in argument but I'm going to make a proffer now, that in 1997, in May, Mr. Rebic meets, in the office of the Presidency of Croatia, with two newspapers. The intent of that meeting is nothing other than to leak -- to take a statement that was provided by Defence counsel to Mr. Rebic and to have it published in the newspapers. It was published two days later. Two weeks later, a Court -- the Blaskic Trial Chamber issues an order which says to the lawyer stop doing this, and it issues broad language, and furthermore all leaks and publications of this material must stop. And now you have these letters which occur after that, which clearly show that he's absorbed what the Trial Chamber had ordered, that he's understanding these protections are in place so he's now including these provisions, so he's reacting to a Trial Chamber's order, so it demonstrates his knowledge that the Trial Chamber is issuing orders beyond closed session, oral orders, and his constructive knowledge therefore of December 1, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Prosecution's case is -- could you wait a minute, Mr. Krsnik. If I understand it correctly, the Prosecution's case is irrespective of various reasons for going into closed session, the effect of closed session would be the same, so the -- Rebic should have understood the meaning of closed session, effect of closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you are going to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: He's in possession of a closed-session transcript, with clear oral orders of a Trial Chamber protecting that witness, which the Appeals Chamber has already ruled that's what happened, and he knows now that there are different implications of that oral order to move into closed session. Very clearly, he's aware that the identity could be protected, the content could be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then only one or a couple of documents will do. Do we need to explore all the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: There's five documents that I'm introducing on that note and the presidential transcript. That's it. That's all I'm intending to do, and that's all I ever intended to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll hear from Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to respond to my learned friend. What he said about the presidential transcript from 1997 is not true at all. The point was that the protected witness, as I read and understand - and I'm trying to clear this up - the protected witness accused late President Tudjman. He, as the president and Supreme Commander of the army, orders and decides and says, "Get hold of that transcript for me." Rebic has nothing to do with that. In that hierarchy, he's somebody somewhere. That is one thing. And the second thing - I won't be long - is the transcript from the closed session was not published in Hrvatski List. What are we discussing then? And we established that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We know that, and as for the first method, I think, Mr. Krsnik, you can cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask a question, Mr. Akerson. In relation to the protected witness we are referring to in tab 18, was -- my question is this: Whether there was a separate protective measures ordered by the Chamber except for the closed session. Was he given a pseudonym or any other protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: My understanding from that stage of the Blaskic trial is that they were not using the procedure of pseudonyms. They were protecting witnesses by going into closed session. I'll double-check that at the break to make sure I'm stating that accurately, but I think at that point in the Blaskic case they weren't using pseudonyms. I know Mr. -- this witness was not given a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In other words, the order simply said closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Correct. That's my understanding. I'll double-check and report back after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'd like -- the Chamber would like you to conclude your examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: One minute. Yes, I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And then we'll deal with the admissibility of the -- of these documents after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'd ask the usher to present to the witness these documents, which are Prosecution Exhibit 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, can you identify this document for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: This is a type signed document from the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please. Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, could you turn on your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a type signed letter from the Assistant Minister of Defence Staff Brigadier Markica Rebic to the Minister of Defence Gojko Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm afraid again that these are conclusions, because on the cover page in Croatian you can see there is no signature and no seal. I think this is an arbitrary conclusion made by the witness as to who it came from. There is no personal signature, no seal, no stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that goes to weight, not admissibility. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by you said -- by saying that it is a type signed letter? I don't follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's language we use -- I apologise for using language that the Court wasn't familiar with, but that's for a document which has the originator in the space where the signature should be but doesn't have a hard copy -- pen signature, actual signature. And we see that quite frequently, because frequently the documents we find in the archives are draft copies or copies which are in the archive of the originator, and frequently, but this isn't the case here, there is documents that are transmitted electronically where there isn't a physical signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is a matter for the weight, so please go on. We'll deal with the whole issue later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The letterhead of this document, what does -- what does that reflect?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: It's the letterhead of the office of the assistant minister for security of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and also has the appropriate serial number for that office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. In this period, yes, he was the assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this document also has another indication of the protection measures that apply to a witness?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this document a fair and accurate copy of the document that you observed, analysed in the Croatian archive?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Other than, Your Honour, I would now ask that all of these exhibits be moved into evidence, as named by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we have cross-examination, the Chamber is minded to take a break, and I was advised to take a break at least for half an hour. So we will adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Prosecution has tendered five documents during the examination-in-chief, and the Chamber will admit them all except for the first one, being P7, the transcript, for the time being. We will make the determination after hearing the cross-examination. Now it is time for the Defence to cross-examine the witness. My English was not clear. Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to report, as I promised, on the protections in the Blaskic case, that there are in fact -- I was incorrect, there are additional protections. There were written decisions for witnesses. Pertaining to the witnesses in the documents I presented, there was, I believe, one written additional protection measure, but I don't know -- I didn't get a chance to look at the date of that. I know there is a written decision and I can report later on the specific date. I just know there was a decision that was issued but I don't know the nature of it. I was just able to get to the index in the short period we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what I announced is that we admit the four documents, which are P16, 17, 18 and 20, and we will deal with the admission of P7 after the cross-examination. Having said that, the numbers should be given to those four exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Pursuant to your decision, Exhibit P16 will be allocated OTP 18. The Exhibit P17 will be allocated the Exhibit OTP 19. The Exhibit P18 will be allocated the Exhibit OTP 20; and finally, the Exhibit P20 will be allocated OTP 21, bearing in mind that all those documents have an English translation, which reads respectively, OTP 18/E, OTP 19/E, OTP 20/E, OTP 21/E. I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And I would like to inform the parties at this time that the Chamber has made an arrangement with the Registry that the hearing can be extended to tomorrow, Thursday, for one day, but that's all we can get for the time being. So we have to make our -- do our best to conclude the hearing by tomorrow. Mr. Ivanovic, do you have anything to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do have a few questions that I would like to put to this witness, quite simply to clarify certain dilemmas that came up during his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please. Cross-examined by Mr. Ivanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all I would like to introduce myself to the witness. My name is Marin Ivanovic, and I represent Mr. Marijacic here. I apologise to the interpreters for not speaking into the microphone. My first question is the following: You said that you looked at a great deal of databases, archives of the Republic of Croatia. In these databases is the name of Ivica Marijacic mentioned at all?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: It may well be, but not in any documentation I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any mention of Hrvatski List?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Not the one you're asking about, although there was a newspaper, I think, by the same name in Herzegovina in the mid-1990s. But not the one you're asking about, which I understand was published in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any mention at all of Hrvatski List which is published in Zadar and has been published in Zadar since 2004?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all these archives, did you find any document that would have to do with Mr. Van Kuijk's testimony in closed session?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, I did, as a matter of fact. There's a number of documents concerning that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show me a single one?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I wasn't instructed to bring any, although I could describe them for the Chamber, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to see one such document, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Actually, the documents which I've seen --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just might suggest that maybe the witness could describe the documents and then we could determine whether or not it's worth the time to go and retrieve them from the archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness describe the --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we should do this in private session, though, because I don't know what document he's referring to, and I have no idea whether there's any protections -- I don't know if it pertains to other witnesses as well. I don't know anything about this document. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness will be able to deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just rephrase my question, and then it's going to be much clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statements that you gave in connection with this case, did you mention a single document that had to do with Mr. Van Kuijk?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that in this way we've resolved the matter. In all these documents that were introduced by the honourable Prosecution, have any signs of confidentiality been noted?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: You mean on the document themselves?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes. Many of them did have various grades of secrecy on them, as is almost always the case with all the documentation we've dealt with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period from the 6th of June, 1997, until the end of 1999, was a single letter published about these protected witnesses that we mentioned previously, those that are referred to in these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just going to object. This witness can't testify to that. He's not an expert. He wasn't brought on to testify about Hrvatski List in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Okay. Then I give up on that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, as the witness did his research of these documents, in this transcript there are two newspapers that are mentioned. Was there any mention in this context of Hrvatski List from Zadar?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. Mr. Krsnik. Mr. Akerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I might be able to save some time. I'm willing to stipulate that the documents that Mr. Tomljanovich testified to don't deal directly with Hrvatski List. They deal with the knowledge that Mr. Rebic had but I don't think that questions regarding whether he saw any documents regarding Hrvatski List; he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Mr. Krsnik. Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tomljanovich. I think that you and I know each other, don't we? So there's no need for me to introduce myself. First I'd like to clarify something with you, as I did yesterday with the previous witness. Could I please ask for your statement that you gave to the honourable Prosecution. It is marked -- what's the marking? Could I please ask our friends of the Prosecution to help us if they have Mr. Tomljanovich's statement here, the one that he gave on the 31st of October, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We have copies, or we could put it on the ELMO, either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, do you have it in front of you? Let me just ask you for the sake of authenticity, because I did not see a signature on your statement at all, so I'm asking you, is this your written statement, written statement, written in your own hand, or did somebody actually interview you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, first of all, on the copy I have I do have my signature here at the bottom of the first page, and then I initialed every page subsequent to that. Now, as far as statement written in my own hand, I typed it myself, upon request of Mr. Akerson asking me to address certain topics -- or these topics, basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the only thing I wanted to ask you, just to check things. Now I have to ask you something in general terms. You said that you've got a Ph.D. from Yale University?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're an historian?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Professor Barnes your mentor at Yale? Is that where you got your Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Excuse me, just for the English translation, it's Banac, not Barnes, and yes, he was my doctoral advisor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Who sent you to work in this Office of the Prosecutor? The UN or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Objection. It's outside the scope and totally irrelevant to this hearing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will ask the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in -- I guess it would have been late January 1999, I received a call from one of my colleagues from graduate school who had already obtained employment here, and he called me and said they were interested for more people with -- in more people with the sorts of qualifications he had and would I like to apply, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course I have very good manners and I am a very decent man, so I'll put this question cautiously. All the efforts that you've made here over the past six years, have they been paid from by your UN salary or from someone else?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I've been paid by the UN for the last nearly seven years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I mistaken if I say that at first you were financed by the Soros Foundation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Yes, you would be mistaken. I haven't been paid by the Soros Foundation while I was working here, and I don't think I ever was in the past for any of my academic research either. Actually, I can say that categorically; I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never had any contacts with that foundation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I've had contacts with persons who work with that foundation. Another colleague of mine from graduate school works for the -- I think it's the Soros Foundation, although I'm not sure exactly what body she's working for. And then one of our colleagues in my office just left work here and went over to work for them, for the Soros Foundation, I think, but I haven't talked to him since he's done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've asked you this -- well, you've just given me a clear answer, because you know about the Soros Foundation, the problems they've had from 1990 until 2000 with the Croatian government, but let us move on. Can you tell us what an historian can do who is not an investigator, not a policeman, who does not have a degree in law? What is a person like that doing in the Office of the Prosecutor? What are you doing specifically?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a long answer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Very short. Very short, please. Very short.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, I do a lot of things. I'm not sure I can give a short answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: First of all, what I'm doing in the Prosecutor's office is extremely similar to what I did as an historian, which is in large part going to the archives - in many cases the same archives - I am reviewing large numbers of documents, finding the ones that are relevant, obtaining copies of those documents, and then analysing and reporting on those documents, which is more or less the same thing I did as an historian. We also do reviews of in-house material sometimes as well, which is also very similar to what I did as an historian. As a matter of fact, when we were working in the Croatian archives in 2001, 2002, I was sitting in the same room I was working on my dissertation in 1992 and 1993 with one of the same colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. As far as I know -- I mean, I don't know a single historian who investigates in terms of dealing with criminal matters. Historians deal with a historical approach, not with an approach from the point of view of criminal law. These are two completely different matters.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, there might ---well, there is a number of us working in the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. You introduced yourself here as an investigator or a research officer of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I object to that question. He's not qualified to express an opinion on the difference between law and history, and I don't think it's relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, can you move on to relevant topics for the sake of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour, but I think that cross -- cross-examination is very important, and it's very important to see whether a witness is qualified or not, because all of this speaks of a credit of a witness. It's very clear if a policeman becomes an historian or the other way around. We'll move on. I'm not going to dwell on this any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, straight away. [In English] Put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomljanovich, I'm telling you now that you do not know about the functioning, the hierarchy both of intelligence services, and you also don't know about the functioning of the authorities in the Republic of Croatia up until the death of President Tudjman. So I would like to ask you kindly to look at this sketch which I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must let him answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He put to you that you don't know these matters. Without giving a long answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll give a short answer. First of all, I didn't make this chart. This chart was put to me, but I did not make this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But today you testified to the fact that it was truthful and that that is the way this functions.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: No, I did not. First of all, I stated clearly, if you go back and look at the record, that this is simply for the purposes of showing the subordinations in regards to the correspondence which was going to be used today, and only for that purpose. I mean, if you had wanted, I could draw up a much larger chart with six large and about 20 smaller organisations that were active in the Republic of Croatia in those years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need for that. I just want to find out whether you know about this or whether you do not know about this. Is this chart something that corresponds to the truth or not? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: It corresponds to what it was intended to do, which was to show the relationships between the persons in this letter. It's not intended to be a complete organigramme of the Croatian intelligence organs, I'm sure. And if it were, you'd have to add a lot more than just the UNS on top of the HIS in providing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, please, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be a bit shorter in your answers if at all possible. I am telling you that you painted the wrong picture and it does not reflect the situation at all. So please look at what is on the ELMO now and tell us, is that perhaps the actual state of affairs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: It is true that the UNS was created by the law on the UNS of the 17th of May, 1995, in order to harmonise and coordinate the activities of the various intelligence agencies. The SIS was one of the agencies they were supposed to coordinate. The HIS, on the other hand, was at least legally an integral part of the UNS, along with a number of other offices, which is certainly true, but we could add all sorts of boxes. It is true that the UNS hierarchically did have that position, although in the correspondence we looked at today, nothing was being addressed to the director of the UNS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I maintain that what you're saying is not true, not correct. Therefore, I will ask you, is UNS superior to the assistant minister, Mr. Rebic, the security service SIS, or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Is the UNS subordinated, did you say, to the -- to Markica Rebic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you is it superior to Markica Rebic and the service called SIS.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, to answer that, first of all I am under the impression from the law on the UNS of 1995 that the UNS was created --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Please, Witness, answer me with a yes or no. Be so kind. Do you know, is it superior or isn't it? Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: You can answer yes or no. It's a bit like the question if you've stopped beating your wife. There's a direct line of reporting which goes through the Ministry of Defence, and he is immediately subordinate to the minister of defence. The UNS -- and don't ask me what exactly this means because I don't know exactly, but the UNS is supposed to harmonise and coordinate and oversee the other bodies, but it's not a direct line of subordination. It is a more direct line of subordination from the UNS to the HIS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You hold out yourself all this time to be an expert in what was going on in government and high politics, and you don't know what the word "UNS" means. How can you possibly understand what was going on under them if you don't know that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I wasn't presented as an expert. Second of all, I do understand what the UNS is and we've just been discussing it. You disagree as to whether or not the relationship between the UNS and the SIS was one of direct subordination. That's another matter. If you put documents to me, I could comment on them, but if you're just speaking in vague terms like this, I can only tell you what I have off the top of my head. And certainly as far as my expertise is concerned, I may know more than some of the people in my office about these things but I certainly know a great deal less about these things than your client.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you for a very simple reason, and of course there is a reason why I'm asking you this question, because you testified today to all these documents that were admitted into evidence. I'm asking you from a point of view of common sense, and I expect the same answer. Can Markica Rebic independently, without the approval of UNS or HIS decide anything? For instance, can Markica Rebic decide independently, without UNS or HIS approval, to publish something in the mass media?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, as far as other decisions are made, yes, he could and he did make decisions without conferring with them. And as far as I'm aware at the conversation we were talking about in the transcript, which is, I believe, the 7th of May, 1997, there were no other members of any other -- of the intelligence service. The director of the UNS was not there, and as far as I remember, Miroslav Tudjman was also not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you are saying absolutely does not correspond to reality. It is not true. What was the service that was designated to cooperate with this court in The Hague, and what is the main intelligence service of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, if I may, there was a document which we decided not to enter into evidence which answers that quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I would just like to say, Your Honour, that although this is an interesting discussion, it doesn't, I don't think, really advance what are the issues at trial because Mr. Tomljanovich principally was introducing documents in a foundational way and didn't testify, express an opinion on them, didn't make any conclusions about them, principally said these are true and accurate copies of documents that were in the archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those documents dealt with this somewhat role of Mr. Rebic, and it is for the Defence to clarify that role.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: It's up to you. My point, I guess, is that it doesn't really matter what Mr. Rebic's role was, he was corresponding with it could have anybody, it just happened to be these people, and I wanted you to have their names, which is why I gave you this little chart. But he could have been corresponding with anybody; it's the fact that he was corresponding with this information that was of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will answer the question without making reference to any exhibits. If the question is -- and now I've almost forgotten what the question is, but if the question is which agencies were responsible for the activities we've been talking about today with the assistance -- in terms of assistance of ICTY defendants, then I can tell you that there were a whole number of agencies which were involved. Now, the agency --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Please, Your Honours. Maybe I don't know how to lead this cross-examination. I do come from a civil law system, but I don't want to be lead by the witness. I want short, clear answers. He can tell me "I don't know," and I'll move on. I asked him what is the main intelligence organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness is coming to the answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- you wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A number of agencies were involved. The agency which had a special team set up to do the operative work was the SIS. Now, the agency which was designated as being the carrier of responsibility, or the Croatian term is "nositelj," for all of these operations was the HIS, but involved a number of other institutions as well. They cooperated with the embassy here, they cooperated with the Foreign Ministry, they cooperated with the Office for Cooperation with the ICTY, and I believe a number of other smaller agencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the first name you referred to? NS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry where were we? Which -- I'll have to look at the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "... being the carrier of responsibility, or the Croatian term is"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, the Croatian term is "nositelj." When they have the orders which establish these operations. The HIS is usually referred to as the nositelj, which I assume means -- and I don't know the jargon, I assume that means that they carry a certain ultimate responsibility. However, most of the operative work was being done by a team of persons in the employ of the SIS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us move on, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not taking us anywhere, because I believe that I'm asking very clear questions, and I can see them on the transcript. I'm asking again, and I want a short answer from the witness:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who coordinated? Who was the top, the commanding service in the Republic of Croatia? Do you know that, Witness, or do you not? Croatia, although it was young and a developing country, it had an organised hierarchy and subordination. So I'm asking you, do you know about that hierarchy or not? And I need to know that so we can clarify the role of Mr. Rebic, and I want not your conclusions but facts. Do you know them or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One question at a time. The first question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the witness know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... top of the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who organised everything and who was responsible for everybody.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: As far as I know, with the language you're using, there was no commanding service. If what you're referring to is the UNS, after May 17, 1995, with the responsibility of coordinating and overseeing the intelligence agencies, then it would be the UNS, but that's different from being the commanding service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Haven't you noticed these documents admitted today? Haven't you noticed that Mr. Rebic was sending them to somebody who was above him? Because if he were -- had been independent and capable of deciding himself, he wouldn't have needed to send those reports to anybody.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: There's two things and I'll deal with one first and then the other. First of all, Mr. Rebic, just to be clear, was immediately subordinated to the minister of defence, who at that time was Mr. Susak. Secondly, he was -- all of these agencies and these operations passed information back and forth. They were told to do so and they were supposed to share this information. It's not a question of subordination to the other agencies. As a matter of fact, when the HIS discovered something new, they'd send that information to the SIS. So I think that's -- that's moving sideways rather than up and down, although the relationship with Minister Susak is a relationship of direct subordination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about him being a part of the Ministry of Defence. Of course he was an assistant minister and as such a part of the ministry, but all this time I've been questioning you with the view to clarifying before this Trial Chamber the kind of hierarchy that prevailed in intelligence services. If we establish that, we will be able to come to the role of Mr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, what is the relevance of the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hierarchy's relevant in order to show that Mr. Rebic was not able to decide anything independently on his own. According to the documents that have been now admitted into evidence, we could easily establish that he could not have been part of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's not being suggested by the Prosecution that this shows that he was part of the Defence team, and I can tell you now that it doesn't. So if that's the only point you're interested in, you can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm grateful. Then I'll move on, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all those searches of archives, have you come across information that the Defence team of General Blaskic manipulated journalists and the media?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection to that question. It's totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you would have been delighted to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, maybe, but I wanted to follow the reasoning of the Prosecutor to show that maybe somebody else gave information to newspapers and manipulated them, although maybe it does not have such importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you ask more concrete questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else, apart from intelligence services, who manipulated journalists and newspapers concerning protected witnesses in order to disqualify those witnesses or for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, "manipulate" is an awfully strong word, but I will say that we do have documentation, and it was one of the exhibits we decided not to enter in this case today, that stories to discredit not protected witnesses but potential witnesses in general were planted in the press by Anto Nobilo. At least, according to this documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us now finish with the transcript, because I am expecting this Trial Chamber will admit them. So let us move on to the transcript from the presidential office. And I think I will conclude with that, Your Honours. Did you talk to any live, living participants who attended meetings in the office of the President Tudjman and who are mentioned in the courtroom today until?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Any meetings or the meeting that happened specifically on the May 7th, 1997?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said clearly we talked only about one transcript today. I'm referring only to that one.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: That particular transcript, no, I've never spoken to any of those people. Certainly not about that transcript. Certainly not with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not going to warn you about decency. We all know that President Tudjman has been dead for six years. I asked you about living witnesses. Out of those living, we have Mr. Ivankovic, Rebic, and Tudjen. Why didn't you ask them about the authenticity of the transcript? Aren't they the only ones who could confirm it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a lawyer or leader of an investigation, so I don't make these decisions, but I would imagine - and this wasn't a decision up to me to make - but I would imagine that people who were identified in a document as undertaking actions which at the very least were unethical if not criminal probably wouldn't confirm the contents of that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you violated the limits of decency again. How can you talk about what's unethical or not? But it's a matter for your own -- it's a matter of your own upbringing. Anyway, is there any list on that transcript, list of persons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any audiotape that could confirm the authenticity of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a shorthand note, minutes?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you then claim that it is authentic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned earlier with the collection. I could go into greater detail about the collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you. It is clear to me, and I hope it is clear to the Trial Chamber, that those are your arbitrary conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The witness should able answer the question that's asked of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If there's anything he can add to what he had stated earlier, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I mean, the question was, and I think it's a relevant question for this Court, How do you claim that this is authentic? and then his answer was cut off. I think that's a question that should be heard, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will allow the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would be repeating what I said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is why I interrupted the witness. I heard the witness saying what he just described, so I said okay, okay. Wasn't every session recorded and taped, as you said yourself, a separate entity, separate recording that forms one whole? If the session on the 17th is one event attended by one set of people, and the session of the 18th was another event attended by a different set of people, aren't both of them quite separate things?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to clarify. I allow that the session attended by the American diplomat who made his own notes from which the transcript was made later is one thing, and the transcript may be correct, but that same American diplomat did not attend all 600 sessions, did he?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: No. And I -- I certainly don't want to give the impression that I based my judgement on these transcripts on one witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please answer this: What was Mr. Markica Rebic doing and which position did he occupy in 2000?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I believe from January 1999 to, I think it was either - and I'm not positive, of course - I think January or February 2000 he was employed as an advisor to the president of the Republic of Croatia for security affairs, and I believe that it would have been in early 2000 that he resigned from that position, and I'm not sure what he did after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm telling you that there -- that he's been retired from 2000 onwards. From the beginning of 2000 to this day, Mr. Rebic is a retired general of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in view of the experience that I see you have, whether a retired officer can have ongoing access to secret archives, military secret archives.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: That question involves the rules internal to the Republic of Croatia, which I don't know in any great detail. I do know that persons who have been called for suspect interviews by the OTP have been allowed access to certain materials, including the presidential transcripts, but as far as what the rules are, as far as they're concerned, from their point of view, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the rule of the hand-over, take-over of duty, that all documents bear a number and during -- in the course of transition of duty, they have to be compared and cross-referenced? It's the practice not only in Croatia but all over the world

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understand the question. I assume you mean during the transition of one government to another. When you talk about hand-over or take-over of duty, or one person from one office to another?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation, and I don't know what you heard, but I said clearly transition of duty. So when Markica Rebic is leaving, he has to hand over his duties to somebody else, including the treasury, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, now I understand the question but I don't know the law, or I don't know the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In the course of your research, did you see anything, beginning with the year 2000 until the year 2004, that was published in the media and that could be ascribed to Mr. Rebic? I'm talking about Hrvatski List until 2004, that four-year period.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH
utterances.text: Well, if you're talking specifically about Hrvatski List only in that period, no, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded my examination. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming, and you may now go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As for the transcript, which is P7, although the Chamber will not give it much weight, but it looks to the Chamber to be authentic and to a certain extent relevant, so the Chamber will admit it into evidence. That can be given number 22. And I'd like to ask the Defence whether it is minded to call the witness. Just a second. Before that, I have to ask -- in an orderly manner. I have to ask Mr. Akerson whether you have completed your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: We would rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Marijacic's Defence believes that Rule 98 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Trial Chamber should be applied in this case. In our opinion, the OTP did not manage to prove in proprio motu that Mr. Marijacic had violated in any way any order of this Court. Invoking the ruling of the Appeals Chamber of the 16th, it is quite clear that protective measures relate to closed session. From the statement of the witness we heard today, it is quite clear that evening the Kingdom of the Netherlands itself treated in a different way the session itself as compared to giving of the statement. Rather, the high officer was not involved in giving a statement but in making a statement before the Court itself. Mr. Marijacic, or the incriminated text, did not publish a single word from the closed session of this Tribunal. Therefore, we believe that the situation is such that Rule 98 should be applied here, and we put that to the Honourable Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I assume Mr. Rebic's Defence will put the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes. Yes, we support and join in this request, so I'm not going to take up more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any response from the Prosecution? Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would ask that the Defence attorney's motion be denied; that we have established a prima facie case. What you have in front of you is a correlation and simply a demonstrative aid of evidence in the closed-session testimony and in the witness statement to show the overlap. The order that was violated by Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic, the first order that was violated, is the order -- the oral order to go into closed session that Mr. Rebic and Mr. Marijacic both admit in writing twice that they possessed and that they went ahead and published the material anyways. Now, the order to go in closed session is contained in the document they admit they possess, and it's very clear on the surface of that document that the parties were intending to protect the identity of the witness. Of course, the content of the testimony is inherently protected. They published his witness statement, which is virtually the same, as you can see from that comparison. But you have both of those pieces. You have both the transcript, both the witness statement in evidence. And based on the standard of proof for a 98 bis, the Prosecution would assert that it's very clear that we have established our prima facie case that a crime has been committed. I can also then address the 2001 order very briefly. I mean, many of these arguments are going to be repeated in the closing, but the 2000 order was printed in its entirety by Slobodna Dalmacija. It was repeatedly referred to not only on the cover but in articles. It was the focus of a series of articles that takes place over six weeks. This is a newspaper which is a major newspaper in Croatia, and it was obviously a major story that ran six weeks, and it was a story about the disclosure, the defiant disclosure of material. That's the way it was couched in these stories. Everything was pointing to that 2000 order. So Mr. Marijacic -- it's a very reasonable inference to make that Mr. Marijacic would know specifically about that order, and therefore that order expresses a very general provision at the end that all publication of statements must cease - 2004, 18 - he gets transcript in a statement, he publishes the statement which is covered by the 2000 order. And so Mr. Marijacic not only violated the oral order of the closed-session transcript but he violated the terms of the order that was issued on December 1, 2000. Lastly, Mr. Rebic, as to his violation of that order, Mr. Marijacic in his May 5th article -- I mean, I -- let me just step back one second. We feel very comfortable that it's a very clear establishment based on the closed session order. I'm now moving on to the 2000 order, so this is a secondary argument, but it's clear from their admissions in their written articles that they discuss the protections. They admit deliberating and then deciding to go ahead and publish anyways. So it's a very reasonable inference for you to make that one of the things they would have discussed is the written court order from the Blaskic Trial Chamber that Mr. Marijacic knew specifically about, and therefore Mr. Rebic also knew about it, and they decided to go ahead and publish it, and Mr. Rebic provided the material to a newspaper knowing -- I mean, there's only one reason that you would have provided, or there's one principal reason you would provide it to a newspaper, or I should say it's very clear, when you provide something to a newspaper, that it's very likely to be published. And so the order of 2000 which says that those who publish or those who are responsible are both to be held accountable easily establish a prima facie case against Mr. Rebic under the 2000 order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On a rather separate matter, can I ask you one question. In December -- sorry, November 2004, when this article was published, was there any remaining reason for the protective measure?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: It's quite possible there was not. However, I don't think that on the face of the transcript that that is a determination that these two gentlemen could have made. And secondly, we would argue that it doesn't really matter because the material was protected by court order and that it is not up to a third party to, on their own, sui sponte, lift the protections that were ordered by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Akerson, this is a Tribunal dealing with the most serious crimes imaginable, and I would certainly like to think that if it's going to be dealing with contempt of court, it's dealing with contempt of court where breaching an order really matters, but you're telling me at the moment that there actually was no purpose to the order at the time any alleged breach may have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I am not saying that there wasn't a purpose for that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. But if the Prosecution can't tell us that there was, then the only reasonable inference to draw is that there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I would respond by saying, Your Honour, that we had to contact the witness to ensure that because we don't know, and I think what's facing the Court is the proposition that people on their own can make that determination and decide that the protection should be lifted. It may be appropriate but only after we consult with the attorneys who asked for the protection and the victim himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
