utterances.text: You see, if this case had concerned the divulging of an identity of a person who had been protected for his own personal security reasons, it would be very easy to see that prosecution was merited, perhaps more than merited, to give reassurance to people who come -- are willing to come to the Tribunal that they will be secure if protection's required. But that's not the sort of case we're dealing with here. We're dealing with what might on the face of it be a technical breach because the Prosecution doesn't review protective measures that the Court has imposed, at its request, to decide whether they should continue in force and -- or be reviewed by the Court. You're trying to put the onus on the public in general to come to the Court and have protective measures reviewed before they decide to do anything which might be a technical breach albeit the reason for the protective measures has gone. I appreciate that that's got perhaps very little to do with the decision on whether there's a sufficiency of evidence, but at some stage in these proceedings I have felt that I would have to express my grave concern about whether this has been an appropriate use of the Tribunal's resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll simply respond by saying it's never been our contention in this case that this is an interference with a witness. That would have been a prosecution of a different kind. We're saying it's an interference with the administration of justice, and any time a newspaper publicly and flagrantly flaunts the authority of an order of a Trial Chamber in protecting a witness on its own, that's a serious violation. We consider it to be a very serious violation because that is put into the marketplace and in the public in Croatia at a time especially when we are recruiting witnesses, identifying witnesses for a huge case in Croatia. And what they're saying on the newsstand in bold headlines is that the newspaper, on its own initiative, can decide that protection orders aren't merited and can expose that witness. Whether it's true or not is irrelevant. It's an interference with the administration of justice, not an interference with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that in light of the evidence led so far, there's a prima facie case so -- for the Defence to answer. So the motion from the Defence is hereby denied. So can I now ask the Defence whether it is minded to lead any evidence for the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then the Defence will have to call many more witnesses than it intended to call. At this moment I cannot tell you who all these witnesses will be, but of course these witnesses are going to be those persons who will refute everything that the Prosecution presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would like to know what these witnesses will be dealing with that can't be dealt with through the medium of the witnesses already listed by you. What is it that you're concerned about that you think requires further witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we reserved the day tomorrow, could you please be so kind as to give us enough time to consult, my colleague and myself, so that we could give you a definite answer tomorrow? I'm going to be completely frank and straightforward: When we set out, I was even thinking of not calling a single witness, to tell you the truth. Well, could you please give me enough time by tomorrow so that my colleague and I could discuss the matter, or perhaps -- well, perhaps we'd need a break now so that we talk to our clients and colleagues. Perhaps we could continue in 15 minutes' time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, don't misunderstand the ruling that the Chamber has made. You have mentioned previously that you're from the civil law system, and many lawyers from the civil law system don't understand very well the "no case to answer." It by no means means that the Trial Chamber is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt. It simply means that there is some evidence which you have to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've been appearing before this Court for long enough now, and I think that I do understand, but I don't know if you've understood my point. If you could just give me a short break to discuss this with my colleague and with our clients. Perhaps we're going to reach a decision to give up on all witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your time's up anyway, Mr. Krsnik. You're timing couldn't be better from the point of view of the motion you're making, but Mr. Akerson has something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: If the Defence -- I mean, the Defence did not list any other witnesses except for their client and one additional witness; each of them, if I remember correctly. We would be objecting if they're at this point now, after this long a period of time, seeking to augment the witness list. I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll hear from the Defence as to their position tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
